explanation: Fires on a sub-word fragment in the middle of a long word that has been split into several tokens (e.g. 'supern[at]ant', 'here[ina]fter', 'post-trans[l]ational', 'Concent[r]ations', 'search[eng]ine'). What matters is that the token sits inside a word, after the first piece and before the rest. Whole-word tokens and word-initial tokens give little or nothing.

Fires on tokens in the header or caption area of legal court opinions: words like 'court', 'Appeal', 'MEMORANDUM', 'ORDER', 'OPINION', and the whitespace or commas around case captions and procedural lines. Strength depends on being inside legal or court document boilerplate. Outside legal text it is weak (license boilerplate gives a little).

Fires strongly on many unrelated tokens in many kinds of text: LaTeX argument names, name parts, 'percent', 'reason(s)', 'Wars', 'Manager', chemical acronyms, and more. I see no shared token or context feature, so a new token cannot be predicted to fire.

Fires on a broad mix of tokens that come right after a subject or head noun and continue the phrase: 'of' after 'founder', verbs after a subject noun ('tend', 'caused', 'continues', 'override'), and code or markup continuations like '="' and '(`'. There is no clear single token class. It may be a generic predicate or continuation signal, but it is hard to predict.

Fires on structural punctuation or function tokens that end an introductory clause or heading and set up what follows: ':' plus newlines after 'Example' or 'may refer to', commas after an opening clause, 'of' in 'Description of the Related Art' or 'description of', and '/' path separators in URLs or file paths. It is a loose mix of prose clause boundaries and path separators.

Fires on the first token, or a sub-piece, of a proper name, citation number, URL or digit sequence in unusual contexts: Japanese mid-word kana, the first digit of phone numbers or DOI numbers, 'https', name starts like 'R'(atu) and 'Ry'(land). It is a mixture with no clear unifying rule beyond 'start of a name or number span'.

Fires mainly on the adverb 'already' and the quantifier 'some' (also 'enough', 'actual'), especially before a verb or noun phrase ('already defending', 'some are paid'). There is a scattering of other unrelated tokens such as 'Index', 'Drive', 'Organ' and code tokens.

Fires on the first sub-word piece of a word split into tokens, mostly medical or anatomical terms ('pal'mar, 'pal'pebral, peric'ard'ial, 'cont'ends) and foreign place or proper names ('Lud'wigsfelde, 'Univers'ità, 'Bad'ghis). It responds to a word-initial fragment of a multi-token, often uncommon, word.

Fires on several unrelated things: '.android' in Android XML namespace URLs ('http://schemas.android.com'), inner digits of multi-digit numbers in math problems, 'WARP' or 'Warp', and physics or nature nouns ('pressure', 'wave', 'sand', 'fire'). It is a mixture.

Fires on Spanish or Latin American proper names and place names, especially the token that starts the second part of a name after an earlier part ('Los' Mochis, 'T'amaulipas, 'El' Salvador, 'Enrique' Peña, Luz 'Elena'), plus some Spanish words. It is strongest in Mexican or Central American contexts. Spanish-looking identifiers in code fire weakly.

Fires on a determiner or possessive ('the', 'a', 'your', 'their') right after a preposition or verb of location or movement ('at', 'to', 'from', 'contact', 'tour'), which introduces a named place, venue or institution ('at the park', 'to the hospital', 'from your local'). The location-preposition context is key. A determiner elsewhere is weak.

Fires on a word-initial sub-word piece of technical or biomedical terms split into several tokens ('fol'liculorum, 'spl'enic, 'gran'ul, 'clar'ifiers, 'melan'oma, 'down'link or 'down'-regulation, 'lob'ectomy). There are some offshoots on ordinary words ('subsequent', 'own', 'their'). It mostly tracks the start of a scientific compound or derived word.

Fires on tokens with an 'ob', 'rob' or 'comb' type letter pattern, i.e. a vowel followed by 'b' ('Rob'inson, 'Rob'ert, T'ob'ii, T'ob'acco, w'ob'bling, 'comb'inatorial, 'cob'alt, Z'eb'ulon). The token's spelling, a sub-word piece ending in or containing 'b', is what matters. 'Rob' gives the strongest activations.

Fires on negation words, mainly 'not' (also 'without', '!', 'no'). It is strongest in modal or imperative phrases such as 'you may not use', 'do not', 'hast thou not'. License-boilerplate 'may not' and 'without even the implied warranty' are common top contexts.

Fires on two things: (1) a person's first name, or the first piece of a surname, in historical or notable name lists ('Karl' Liebknecht, 'Ben' Jonson, 'Robert', 'Sam' Adams, Jean-Paul 'Sat're); and (2) the 'hem', 'haem' or 'ha' piece of medical words (haemorrhage, hemophilia, hemodialysis), plus other medical word-initial pieces.

Fires on non-Latin-script tokens (Japanese, Chinese, Devanagari, Cyrillic, Arabic), especially the first non-ASCII token after a switch from English or code context (comments, string literals, parentheses after a name). It is weaker on English words about nationalities or speakers in mid-range examples.

Fires on the opening parenthesis plus variable name of a function definition in synthetic math problems ('Let b(n) = ...'). More moderately, it fires on bound-variable or parameter tokens in code (lambda or LINQ variables, function parameters, loop variables). The function-argument variable after a function name is key.

Fires on separator tokens (double newlines, colons, '**', '»') in list-like, tabular or fragmentary text where short items are separated by blank lines (table headers, menus, dates), and also on sentence-initial 'There' or 'there' and 'also'. It is mostly a document-structure separator detector with odd offshoots.

Fires on sentence-ending or trailing punctuation that closes an exclamation or trailing-off phrase, especially '!' and ellipsis '...' or '[...]' ('enter!', 'free!', 'the question is...', 'read more'). It is moderate on ordinary periods and weak elsewhere.

Fires on a very heterogeneous set of tokens: Hungarian and Albanian word pieces, music-related words ('melody', 'timbres', 'Subtone'), function words ('and', 'that', 'of', 'but'), and years. I find no consistent rule.

Fires on the first token of a distinctive, fairly rare content word or name that names a topical entity: conflict or political groups ('Donetsk', 'Hezbollah', 'Hamas', 'WikiLeaks'), Java or Python package names after 'import org.' ('.jetbrains', '.slf', 'shutil', 'timedelta'), and emotionally loaded words ('drunken', 'upheaval', 'procrast', 'tantrum'). It is a mixture.
